Why it matters
Why it matters

Service is what we do for the guest. Hospitality is how the guest feels while we do it.

The business case
  • Guests visit the first time for many reasons
  • They return for one: they liked the food, the place and the people
  • Repeat guests cost less to win and spend more over time
  • Consistency, not one great night, builds that loyalty

The nine principles are the habits that make guests feel looked after, every visit.

Principles 1–3
Principles 1–3

Welcome, know, deliver.

01 · WelcomingGreeting and farewell

A warm, sincere greeting tells guests they can relax. A warm farewell invites them back.

02 · KnowledgeableThe question behind the question

Know the menu, ingredients and venue well enough to answer what the guest really wants to find out.

03 · EfficientSmooth, quick, calm

When guests see a team moving with ease, they feel at ease. And it gives us more time for each table.

Role play · Knowledgeable
The guestDining with her young son
Role play
The question behind the question.

"Is this spicy?" may really mean "Will I enjoy this?" or "Is it safe for my child?"

GuestIs this dish spicy?
Server · SaraIt has a gentle warmth from the chilli oil. Are you asking for yourself, or for the little one?
GuestFor my son. He doesn't like anything hot.
Server · SaraThen I'd serve the chilli oil on the side, so he can enjoy it mild and you can add as much as you like.
GuestPerfect, thank you.
Principle 1 · Welcoming
Principle 1 · Welcoming

First and last impressions.

Always

  • Acknowledge every guest within 10 seconds of arrival
  • Smile, make eye contact, greet in the guest's preferred language
  • Use the guest's name when you know it
  • Walk guests to the door when the floor allows
  • Thank guests sincerely and invite them back

Never

  • Keep guests waiting without acknowledgement
  • Greet while looking at a screen or phone
  • Use a scripted, flat welcome
  • Let the bill be the last interaction
  • Start clearing or resetting during the goodbye
Principle 4 · Well timed
Principle 4 · Well timed

Anticipate before they ask.

1
Arrival

Water and menus as guests settle; offer drinks without delay.

2
Ordering

Approach when menus close or guests look up.

3
During

Refill, replace cutlery and clear before the guest notices.

4
Pace

Read the table: lunch meeting or celebration?

5
Departure

Have the bill ready when guests signal.

Principles 5–7
Principles 5–7

Adapt, repeat, communicate.

05 · FlexibleStandards serve guests

Adapt the experience whenever safety, quality and the kitchen allow it.

06 · ConsistentSame standard, every time

Every visit, shift and table. The only reliable way to build repeat business.

07 · Communicates wellRight information, right moment

Simple and tactful. Help the guest decide; never lecture or talk down.

Principle 5 · Flexible
Principle 5 · Flexible

Say yes whenever standards, safety and the kitchen allow it, and offer an alternative when they do not.

Examples of flexibility
  • Individual portions in a sharing-style concept
  • Adjusting spice level, or sauce on the side
  • Moving a guest to a quieter table
  • Pacing courses slower or faster on request

The limit: never bend allergen, licensing or safety rules. If unsure, ask the manager on duty before you promise.

Principles 8–9
Principles 8–9

Earn trust, then go further.

08 · Instils trustThe foundation

Dishes described accurately, allergens handled correctly, hygiene standards met.

09 · Goes furtherSmall, personal touches

A remembered name or usual drink, something for a child, a gesture beyond the apology.

In practiceWithin the rules

Gestures follow the complimentary policy. Agree them with the manager on duty.

Principle 8 · Trust
Principle 8 · Trust

How guests learn to trust us.

  • Dishes described exactly as they arrive
  • Allergen questions checked with the kitchen, never guessed
  • Clean uniforms, hands, menus and tables
  • Honest wait times, and updates if they change
  • Accurate bills, explained when asked
  • Promises kept: if you say you'll check, you check
  • Mistakes admitted quickly and put right
  • Guest information kept confidential

Principles in action

Which principle applies?

SituationPrincipleRight response
A first-time guest looks lost at the doorWelcomingGreet immediately, introduce yourself, guide them in
A guest asks if a dish contains nutsTrust · KnowledgeableConfirm with the kitchen, then answer clearly
A table of four wants their own platesFlexibleOffer individual portions or suggested pairings
A business guest has 45 minutesWell timed · EfficientRecommend quick dishes, present the bill early
A regular's usual drink is knownGoes furtherOffer it by name as they sit down
The kitchen is running lateCommunicates wellInform the table early, apologise, give a realistic time
